claim: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria with a unique CO2 concentrating mechanism (CCM).
source: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria with a unique CO2 concentrating mechanism (CCM), enhancing carbon fixation.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about cyanobacteria presented in the abstract.

claim: The CCM enhances carbon fixation in cyanobacteria.
source: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria with a unique CO2 concentrating mechanism (CCM), enhancing carbon fixation.
evidence: This is stated as a known function of the CCM.

claim: Efficiency of the CCM requires saturating the RuBisCO reaction.
source: Efficiency requires saturating the RuBisCO reaction, staying below saturation for carbonic anhydrase, and avoiding wasteful oxygenation reactions.
evidence: This is a criterion for efficiency defined by the authors based on their model analysis.

claim: Efficiency of the CCM requires staying below saturation for carbonic anhydrase.
source: Efficiency requires saturating the RuBisCO reaction, staying below saturation for carbonic anhydrase, and avoiding wasteful oxygenation reactions.
evidence: This is a criterion for efficiency defined by the authors based on their model analysis.

claim: Efficiency of the CCM requires avoiding wasteful oxygenation reactions.
source: Efficiency requires saturating the RuBisCO reaction, staying below saturation for carbonic anhydrase, and avoiding wasteful oxygenation reactions.
evidence: This is a criterion for efficiency defined by the authors based on their model analysis.

claim: Selectivity at the carboxysome shell is not necessary for CCM function.
source: We find selectivity at the carboxysome shell is not necessary; there is an optimal non-specific carboxysome shell permeability.
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is an optimal non-specific carboxysome shell permeability.
source: We find selectivity at the carboxysome shell is not necessary; there is an optimal non-specific carboxysome shell permeability.
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: At the optimal carboxysome permeability, contributions from CO2 scavenging at the cell membrane are small.
source: At the optimal carboxysome permeability, contributions from CO2 scavenging at the cell membrane are small.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Carboxysomes are small, 100–200 nm compartments.
source: These small, 100–200 nm compartments separate the principal reaction of the Calvin cycle, the RuBisCO catalyzed fixation of carbon dioxide (CO2) into 3-phosphoglycerate, from the rest of the cell (Cannon et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a known structural characteristic of carboxysomes supported by citation.

claim: Carboxysomes separate the RuBisCO catalyzed fixation of CO2 into 3-phosphoglycerate from the rest of the cell.
source: These small, 100–200 nm compartments separate the principal reaction of the Calvin cycle, the RuBisCO catalyzed fixation of carbon dioxide (CO2) into 3-phosphoglycerate, from the rest of the cell (Cannon et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a known function of carboxysomes supported by citation.

claim: CO2 and O2 competitively bind as substrates of RuBisCO.
source: CO2 and oxygen (O2) competitively bind as substrates of RuBisCO, and the reaction with O2 produces phosphoglycolate, a waste product which must be recycled by the cell (Jordan & Ogren, 1981; Tcherkez et al., 2006; Savir et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a known biochemical property of RuBisCO supported by citations.

claim: The reaction of RuBisCO with O2 produces phosphoglycolate, a waste product which must be recycled by the cell.
source: CO2 and oxygen (O2) competitively bind as substrates of RuBisCO, and the reaction with O2 produces phosphoglycolate, a waste product which must be recycled by the cell (Jordan & Ogren, 1981; Tcherkez et al., 2006; Savir et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a known biochemical consequence of RuBisCO oxygenation supported by citations.

claim: The carboxysome is believed to act as a diffusion barrier to CO2.
source: To maximize carboxylation and minimize oxygenation, the carboxysome is believed to act as a diffusion barrier to CO2 (Reinhold et al., 1989; Dou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about carboxysome function supported by citations.

claim: Inorganic carbon concentration in cyanobacteria is elevated well above 200–300 μM, the CO2 concentration required for saturating RuBisCO.
source: Due to this mechanism, inorganic carbon concentration is elevated well above 200–300 μM, the CO2 concentration required for saturating the RuBisCO.
evidence: This is a known effect of the CCM.

claim: Concentrations of 20–40 mM inorganic carbon, up to 4000-fold higher than external levels, have been observed in cyanobacteria.
source: Concentrations of 20–40 mM inorganic carbon, up to 4000-fold higher than external levels, have been observed (Kaplan & Reinhold, 1999; Woodger et al., 2005; Sultemeyer et al., 1995; Price et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by multiple citations.

claim: The bilipid outer and cell membranes are highly permeable to small uncharged molecules such as CO2.
source: The bilipid outer and cell membranes are highly permeable to small uncharged molecules such as CO2 (Missner et al., 2008; Gutknecht et al., 1977), so instead the cell primarily accumulates the charged and less membrane soluble bicarbonate (HCO3−) (Volokita et al., 1984; Price & Badger, 1989).
evidence: This is a known property of biological membranes supported by citations.

claim: The cell primarily accumulates the charged and less membrane soluble bicarbonate (HCO3−).
source: The bilipid outer and cell membranes are highly permeable to small uncharged molecules such as CO2 (Missner et al., 2008; Gutknecht et al., 1977), so instead the cell primarily accumulates the charged and less membrane soluble bicarbonate (HCO3−) (Volokita et al., 1984; Price & Badger, 1989).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citations.

claim: Active transporters, both constitutive and inducible, bring HCO3− into the cell.
source: Active transporters, both constitutive and inducible, bring HCO3− into the cell (Price et al., 2008, 2004; Omata et al., 1999), and mechanisms exist to actively convert CO2 to HCO3− at the thylakoid and cell membrane (Price et al., 2008; Maeda et al., 2002; Shibata et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a known mechanism of the CCM supported by citations.

claim: Mechanisms exist to actively convert CO2 to HCO3− at the thylakoid and cell membrane.
source: Active transporters, both constitutive and inducible, bring HCO3− into the cell (Price et al., 2008, 2004; Omata et al., 1999), and mechanisms exist to actively convert CO2 to HCO3− at the thylakoid and cell membrane (Price et al., 2008; Maeda et al., 2002; Shibata et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a known mechanism of the CCM supported by citations.

claim: Once HCO3− passively diffuses into the carboxysome, it is rapidly brought into equilibrium with CO2 by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.
source: Once it passively diffuses into the carboxysome, HCO3− is rapidly brought into equilibrium with CO2 by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, resulting in the production of CO2 near RuBisCO.
evidence: This is a known mechanism of the CCM.

claim: Carbonic anhydrase is known to be localized on the interior side of the carboxysome shell.
source: Carbonic anhydrase is known to be localized on the interior side of the carboxysome shell (Yeates et al., 2008; Cannon et al., 1991; Cot et al., 2008; Long et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a known structural feature supported by citations.

claim: Visualizations of the location of the carboxysomes with fluorescent microscopy in Synechococcus elongatus PCC7942 demonstrated that the carboxysomes are evenly spaced along the centerline of the cell.
source: Visualizations of the location of the carboxysomes with fluorescent microscopy in Synechococcus elongatus PCC7942 demonstrated that the carboxysomes are evenly spaced along the centerline of the cell, (Savage et al., 2010), raising the question of how spatial organization, beyond simple partitioning, changes the efficacy of the system.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation.

claim: The model treats a spherically symmetric cell, with one carboxysome at the center.
source: The model treats a spherically symmetric cell, with one carboxysome at the center.
evidence: This is a description of the model setup shown in Figure 1.

claim: The carboxysome shell must be permeable enough to allow HCO3− and 3-phosphoglycerate to readily diffuse in and out.
source: The carboxysome shell must be permeable enough to allow HCO3− and 3-phosphoglycerate to readily diffuse in and out.
evidence: This is a functional requirement inferred from the system's operation.

claim: The HCO3− concentration in the cytosol is constant across the cell, set by the HCO3− transport and leakage rates.
source: We find that the HCO3− concentration in the cytosol is constant across the cell, set by the HCO3− transport and leakage rates, and depends very little on the carboxysome permeability.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The HCO3− concentration in the cytosol depends very little on the carboxysome permeability.
source: We find that the HCO3− concentration in the cytosol is constant across the cell, set by the HCO3− transport and leakage rates, and depends very little on the carboxysome permeability.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The carboxysome permeability sets how the CO2 is partitioned between the carboxysome and cytosol.
source: The carboxysome permeability does, however, set how the CO2 is partitioned between the carboxysome and cytosol.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: At optimal carboxysome permeability, HCO3− diffusion into the carboxysome is fast enough to supply inorganic carbon for fixation, but the rate of CO2 leakage out of the carboxysome is low.
source: At optimal carboxysome permeability, HCO3− diffusion into the carboxysome is fast enough to supply inorganic carbon for fixation, but the rate of CO2 leakage out of the carboxysome is low.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis explaining the optimal permeability.

claim: Concentration of carbonic anhydrase increases the maximum rate of reaction for carbonic anhydrase per volume.
source: Concentration of carbonic anhydrase increases the maximum rate of reaction for carbonic anhydrase per volume, causing carbonic anhydrase to saturate at a higher level of HCO3−, and achieve an order of magnitude higher local CO2 concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Concentrating carbonic anhydrase causes it to saturate at a higher level of HCO3−.
source: Concentration of carbonic anhydrase increases the maximum rate of reaction for carbonic anhydrase per volume, causing carbonic anhydrase to saturate at a higher level of HCO3−, and achieve an order of magnitude higher local CO2 concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Concentrating carbonic anhydrase achieves an order of magnitude higher local CO2 concentrations.
source: Concentration of carbonic anhydrase increases the maximum rate of reaction for carbonic anhydrase per volume, causing carbonic anhydrase to saturate at a higher level of HCO3−, and achieve an order of magnitude higher local CO2 concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Encapsulation of the reactions in an optimally permeable carboxysome shell achieves another order of magnitude of CO2 concentration.
source: Encapsulation of the reactions in an optimally permeable carboxysome shell achieves another order of magnitude of CO2 concentration.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The model solves for both the HCO3− and CO2 concentration throughout a spherical cell.
source: Our three dimensional model of the CCM solves for both the HCO3− and CO2 concentration throughout a spherical cell.
evidence: This is a description of the model.

claim: The model considers a spherical cell of radius Rb = 0.5 μm with a single spherical carboxysome of radius Rc = 50 nm containing RuBisCO and carbonic anhydrase.
source: We solve this model numerically and analytically at steady state for three different spatial organizations of carbonic anhydrase and RuBisCO in the cell (See Figure 6): enzymes distributed evenly throughout the cell, enzymes localized to the center of the cell but not encapsulated (as they would be on a scaffold), enzymes encapsulated in a carboxysome. We compare the effects of these scenarios in the discussion section, and for now consider a spherical cell of radius Rb = 0.5 μm with a single spherical carboxysome of radius Rc = 50 nm containing RuBisCO and carbonic anhydrase.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: Crystal structures show the carboxysome surface has approximately Npores = 4800 small pores with radius rpore ≈ 0.35 nm, and thickness l = 1.8 nm.
source: Crystal structures (Yeates et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2008; yeates et al., 2007) show the surface has approximately Npores = 4800 small pores with radius rpore≈0.35 nm, and thickness l = 1.8 nm.
evidence: This is structural information from crystal structures supported by citations.

claim: There is a crescent shaped region in parameter space where the CCM is effective.
source: There is a crescent shaped region between these regions, where the CCM is effective according to our criteria.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and described in the text.

claim: Any combination of jc and kc which produce C = C99%, make 133 times more CO2 available in the carboxysome than there is total inorganic carbon outside the cell.
source: Any combination of jc and kc which produce C = C99%, make 133 times more CO2 available in the carboxysome than there is total inorganic carbon outside the cell.
evidence: This is calculated from the model results.

claim: When jc is low, the ratio of CO2 and HCO3− is constant, set by the chemical equilibrium at a given pH.
source: When jc is low, the ratio of CO2 and HCO3− is constant, set by the chemical equilibrium at a given pH.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: For each line of constant concentration in Figure 2 there is an optimal permeability value, where the least HCO3− transport is required to achieve the same CO2 concentration.
source: For each line of constant concentration in Figure 2 there is an optimal permeability value, where the least HCO3− transport is required to achieve the same CO2 concentration.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: At high permeability, the CO2 produced in the carboxysome rapidly leaks out of the carboxysome.
source: At high permeability, the CO2 produced in the carboxysome rapidly leaks out of the carboxysome, and the CO2 concentration in the cytosol, shown in Figure 4D, is relatively high.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When the carboxysome permeability decreases to near the optimal value, the carboxysome traps CO2, and the cytosolic levels are lower, decreasing leakage out of the cell.
source: When the carboxysome permeability decreases to near the optimal value, Figure 4C, the carboxysome traps CO2, and the cytosolic levels are lower, decreasing leakage out of the cell.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The transition from high to optimal permeability occurs when diffusion across the cell (and carboxysome) takes a shorter time than diffusion through the carboxysome shell.
source: This transition occurs when diffusion across the cell (and carboxysome) takes a shorter time than diffusion through the carboxysome shell; or the CO2 in the carboxysome is effectively partitioned from the CO2 in the cell.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism from the model analysis.

claim: At low external inorganic carbon conditions, internal inorganic carbon pools due to CCM activity are regularly measured as high as Ci = 30 mM.
source: At low external inorganic carbon conditions, internal inorganic carbon pools due to CCM activity are regularly measured as high as Ci = 30 mM.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citations.

claim: The inorganic carbon is predominantly in the form of HCO3−.
source: The inorganic carbon is predominantly in the form of HCO3−, and measurements do not distinguish between the cytosol and carboxysome (Kaplan & Reinhold, 1999; Woodger et al., 2005; Sultemeyer et al., 1995; Price et al., 1998, 2008).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citations.

claim: Measurements do not distinguish between the cytosol and carboxysome.
source: The inorganic carbon is predominantly in the form of HCO3−, and measurements do not distinguish between the cytosol and carboxysome (Kaplan & Reinhold, 1999; Woodger et al., 2005; Sultemeyer et al., 1995; Price et al., 1998, 2008).
evidence: This is a limitation of experimental measurements noted by the authors.

claim: The cytosolic HCO3− concentration is 30 mM when jc = 0.6 cm/s, over a wide range of the carboxysome permeability.
source: In our model, we find that the cytosolic HCO3− concentration is 30 mM when jc=0.6cms, over a wide range of the carboxysome permeability (indicated as the dashed grey line in Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The cytosolic HCO3− concentration is the dominate form of inorganic carbon in the cell at jc = 0.6 cm/s.
source: From Figure 4 we can also see that the cytosolic HCO3− concentration is the dominate form of inorganic carbon in the cell at jc=0.6cms.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For cells grown under low inorganic carbon conditions net HCO3− fluxes are measured 105 pmol/(mg Chl s).
source: For cells grown under low inorganic carbon conditions net HCO3− fluxes (transport - leakage) are measured 105pmolmgChls, with CO2 net flux being slightly lower but the same order of magnitude (Whitehead et al., 2014; Badger et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement supported by citations.

claim: CO2 net flux is slightly lower but the same order of magnitude as HCO3− net flux.
source: For cells grown under low inorganic carbon conditions net HCO3− fluxes (transport - leakage) are measured 105pmolmgChls, with CO2 net flux being slightly lower but the same order of magnitude (Whitehead et al., 2014; Badger et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citations.

claim: High external inorganic carbon conditions produce slightly higher net HCO3− rates.
source: High external inorganic carbon conditions produce slightly higher net HCO3− rates (Tchernov et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation.

claim: The net HCO3− flux for the model cell is 6 × 10−6 pmol/(cell s).
source: The net HCO3− flux for our model cell is 6×10−6pmol(cells), so we are about an order of magnitude too high.
evidence: This is calculated from the model.

claim: The model net HCO3− flux is about an order of magnitude too high compared to experimental measurements.
source: The net HCO3− flux for our model cell is 6×10−6pmol(cells), so we are about an order of magnitude too high.
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data.

claim: According to the calculation only around 1% of the carbon transported into the cell is fixed into 3-phosphoglycerate.
source: According to our calculation only around 1 % of the carbon transported into the cell is fixed into 3-phosophoglycerate.
evidence: This is calculated from the model results shown in Table 3.

claim: Even in this highly CO2 concentrating regime, 5 × 104 2-phosphoglycolate are produced per second.
source: Even in this highly CO2 concentrating regime, 5 × 104 2-phosophoglycolate produced per second.
evidence: This is calculated from the model results.

claim: Cyanobacteria have been shown to have multiple pathways for recycling 2-phosphoglycolate.
source: Cyanobacteria have been shown to have multiple pathways for recycling 2-phosophoglycolate (Hackenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a known feature of cyanobacterial metabolism supported by citation.

claim: The system fixes CO2 at a rate of 0.14 pg/hour.
source: Our system fixes CO2 at a rate of 0.14 pg/hour.
evidence: This is calculated from the model results.

claim: Between 115–300 fg/μm3 of carbon are needed to produce a new cyanobacterial cell.
source: Given the volume of our cell, and the fact that between 115–300 fg/μm3 of carbon are needed to produce a new cyanobacterial cell (Mahlmann et al., 2008) we need between 0.1 and 0.3 picograms of carbon per cell.
evidence: This is a known requirement for cell division supported by citation.

claim: At the higher flux rate a cell could replicate every 7–21 hr.
source: At the higher flux rate (Table 3) this means that a cell could replicate every 7–21 hr and the lower flux rate (Table 4) allows replication every 11–35 hr.
evidence: This is calculated from the model results and carbon requirements.

claim: At the lower flux rate a cell could replicate every 11–35 hr.
source: At the higher flux rate (Table 3) this means that a cell could replicate every 7–21 hr and the lower flux rate (Table 4) allows replication every 11–35 hr.
evidence: This is calculated from the model results and carbon requirements.

claim: Both replication times are consistent with the division times of cyanobacteria.
source: Both are consistent with the division times of cyanobacteria.
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with known biological data.

claim: The incoming inorganic carbon source for the carboxysome system is invariant with the position of the carboxysome in the cell.
source: This means the incoming inorganic carbon source for the carboxysome system is invariant with the position of the carboxysome in the cell.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: There is a gradient in CO2 concentration across the cell when the carboxysome permeability is at or above the optimum.
source: In contrast, there is a gradient in CO2 concentration across the cell when the carboxysome permeability is at or above the optimum (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The cell membrane is more permeable to CO2 than to HCO3−.
source: The cell membrane is more permeable to CO2.
evidence: This is a known property of biological membranes.

claim: Moving the carboxysome close to the cell membrane increases the leakage rate of CO2 out of the carboxysome.
source: The gradient means that the CO2 leakage out of the cell affects the CO2 leakage out of the carboxysome. Moving the carboxysome close to the cell membrane increases the leakage rate of CO2 out of the carboxysome.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: In S. elongatus the carboxysomes are located along the center line of the cell, away from the cell membranes.
source: Notably, in S. elongatus the carboxysomes are located along the center line of the cell, away from the cell membranes (Savage et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation.

claim: The local concentration of CO2 is higher near a carboxysome.
source: In fact, since the local concentration of CO2 is higher near a carboxysome, nearby carboxysomes would 'feed' each other CO2.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Nearby carboxysomes would 'feed' each other CO2.
source: In fact, since the local concentration of CO2 is higher near a carboxysome, nearby carboxysomes would 'feed' each other CO2.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Clumping of carboxysomes would reduce the probability of distributing carboxysomes equitably to daughter cells.
source: As has been shown, such clumping would reduce the probability of distributing carboxysomes equitably to daughter cells, possibly counteracting any benefit (Savage et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a known consequence of carboxysome clumping supported by citation.

claim: The concentration across the carboxysome is basically constant.
source: The concentration across the carboxysome is basically constant, because the carboxysome is so small that diffusion across it takes very little time.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The carboxysome is so small that diffusion across it takes very little time.
source: The concentration across the carboxysome is basically constant, because the carboxysome is so small that diffusion across it takes very little time.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the model analysis.

claim: The organization of the reactions in the carboxysome does not affect the CO2 concentration in the carboxysome.
source: A consequence of this is that the organization of the reactions in the carboxysome does not effect the CO2 concentration in the carboxysome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The localization of the carbonic anhydrase to the inner carboxysome shell seems to have no effect on the CCM.
source: Therefore, the localization of the carbonic anhydrase to the inner carboxysome shell seems to have no effect on the CCM.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: It has been suggested that diffusion in the carboxysome should be slower, since the carboxysome is packed with RuBisCO.
source: It has been suggested that diffusion in the carboxysome should be slower, since the carboxysome is packed with RuBisCO.
evidence: This is a hypothesis mentioned by the authors.

claim: If the diffusion is indeed slower in the carboxysome it does not aid the CCM.
source: So if the diffusion is indeed slower in the carboxysome it does not aid the CCM.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: Even at slower diffusion, the CO2 concentration across the carboxysome is flat.
source: Even at this slower diffusion, the CO2 concentration across the carboxysome is flat.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Increasing conversion, α > 0, can facilitate uptake of CO2 from outside the cell and scavenge CO2 escaped from the carboxysome.
source: Increasing conversion, α > 0, can facilitate uptake of CO2 from outside the cell and scavenge CO2 escaped from the carboxysome.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Scavenging broadens the range of carboxysome permeability which will effectively separate the inorganic carbon pools in the carboxysome and outside.
source: Scavenging broadens the range of carboxysome permeability which will effectively separate the inorganic carbon pools in the carboxysome and outside.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Neither facilitated uptake nor scavenging effects are particularly strong in the current range of reaction rates and cell membrane permeability.
source: However, neither of these effects is particularly strong in our current range of reaction rates, and cell membrane permeability (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The relative effect of facilitated uptake and scavenging depends on the external CO2 and HCO3− concentrations.
source: The relative effect of these two mechanisms depends on the external CO2 and HCO3− concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: In saltwater environments the pH is near 8 and HCO3− is the predominant inorganic carbon source.
source: In saltwater environments the pH is near 8 and HCO3− is the predominant inorganic carbon source.
evidence: This is a known environmental condition.

claim: The effect of facilitated uptake under oceanic conditions is very small.
source: The effect of facilitated uptake, under these assumptions, is very small.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: In freshwater or under conditions of ocean acidification, where the pH could fall to 6 or lower, there can be a much larger proportion of CO2 (>50%).
source: In freshwater or under conditions of ocean acidification, where the pH could fall to 6 or lower, there can be a much larger proportion of CO2 (>50%).
evidence: This is a known environmental condition.

claim: Even though the same velocity of facilitated uptake and HCO3− transport is assumed, facilitated uptake contributes less because it is limited by CO2 diffusion across the membrane.
source: Even though we assume the same velocity of facilitated uptake and HCO3− transport (jc=αKα=1), facilitated uptake contributes less because it is limited by CO2 diffusion across the membrane.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: At the same rates of transport the facilitated uptake mechanism only contributes more than active HCO3− if the CO2 concentration is greater than 80% of external inorganic carbon.
source: At the same rates of transport the facilitated uptake mechanism only contributes more than active HCO3− if the CO2 concentration is greater than 80% of external inorganic carbon.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Oceanic cyanobacteria such as Prochlorococcus only seem to possess gene homologs for HCO3− transport systems.
source: This is consistent with observations that oceanic cyanobacteria such as Prochlorococcus only seem to possess gene homologs for HCO3− transport systems, while other freshwater and estuarine cyanobacteria have gene homologs for both constitutive (NDH-14) and inducible (NDH-13) CO2 uptake systems as well as inducible HCO3− transport systems (BicA, SbtA, and BCT1) (Price, 2011).
evidence: This is a known genomic observation supported by citation.

claim: Freshwater and estuarine cyanobacteria have gene homologs for both constitutive (NDH-14) and inducible (NDH-13) CO2 uptake systems as well as inducible HCO3− transport systems (BicA, SbtA, and BCT1).
source: This is consistent with observations that oceanic cyanobacteria such as Prochlorococcus only seem to possess gene homologs for HCO3− transport systems, while other freshwater and estuarine cyanobacteria have gene homologs for both constitutive (NDH-14) and inducible (NDH-13) CO2 uptake systems as well as inducible HCO3− transport systems (BicA, SbtA, and BCT1) (Price, 2011).
evidence: This is a known genomic observation supported by citation.

claim: It is possible that since the scavenging mechanism is associated with the electron transport chain of the light reactions of photosynthesis scavenging can be ramped up more easily when there is excess light energy.
source: It is possible that since the scavenging mechanism is associated with the electron transport chain of the light reactions of photosynthesis scavenging can be ramped up more easily when there is excess light energy.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors.

claim: It has been suggested that the cell uses the scavenging mechanism as a way to dissipate excess light energy.
source: Indeed it has been suggested that the cell uses this mechanism as a way to dissipate excess light energy (Tchernov et al., 1997, 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Concentrating carbonic anhydrase and RuBisCO to a small region in the center of the cell leads to an order of magnitude increase in the concentration of CO2.
source: Concentrating carbonic anhydrase and RuBisCO to a small region in the center of the cell, on a scaffold for example, leads to an order of magnitude increase in the concentration of CO2.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Localizing the carbonic anhydrase to a small volume concentrates it, increasing the maximum reaction rate per volume, Vca and Vba.
source: Localizing the carbonic anhydrase to a small volume concentrates it, increasing the maximum reaction rate per volume, Vca and Vba.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism from the model analysis.

claim: A larger Vba increases the HCO3− concentration at which carbonic anhydrase is saturated allowing the mechanism to take advantage of a larger HCO3− flux, jc.
source: A larger Vba increases the HCO3− concentration at which carbonic anhydrase is saturated allowing the mechanism to take advantage of a larger HCO3− flux, jc.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism from the model analysis.

claim: A small increase can be gained from encapsulating the enzymes in a permeable carboxysome shell.
source: A small increase can be gained from encapsulating the enzymes in a permeable carboxysome shell and another order of magnitude is gained at the optimal permeability.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Another order of magnitude is gained at the optimal permeability.
source: A small increase can be gained from encapsulating the enzymes in a permeable carboxysome shell and another order of magnitude is gained at the optimal permeability.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: At optimal carboxysome permeability, the CO2 is effectively partitioned into the carboxysome and conversion can act only as facilitated uptake.
source: At optimal carboxysome permeability, the CO2 is effectively partitioned into the carboxysome and conversion can act only as facilitated uptake as shown in Figure 5.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The futile cycle is most detrimental when the enzymes are distributed throughout the cytosol, and increases the oxygenation error rate.
source: The futile cycle is most detrimental when the enzymes are distributed through out the cytosol, and increases the oxygenation error rate (data not shown).
